records.story: Mellow Corn was first made in 1945 by the Medley Distilling Company of Owensboro, Kentucky, and went out under a yellow, red and green label bearing the Medley family crest. In 1993, by Heaven Hill's own account, the brand came to Heaven Hill of Bardstown in a deal for several labels with United Distillers. Heaven Hill changed almost nothing. The label stayed as it was, its people having decided long ago not to touch it, and the whiskey kept to the bonded rule: one distilling season, four years in a bonded warehouse, 100 proof. It stood on the low shelves of the markets that already knew it, and for decades, in Heaven Hill's telling, it was the one aged corn whiskey sold across the country. Then bartenders found it, drawn first by the loud label and kept by the grain, and Heaven Hill's own ambassador built a highball on it, the Meloma, a Paloma made with corn whiskey in place of tequila. In 2023 the house showed the same recipe at twenty years old in its Heritage Collection. For a bartender Mellow Corn is the plain lesson in what separates corn whiskey from bourbon: the same grain, but oak that has held whiskey before.

records.story: Georgia Moon takes its name from the moonshiners of corn whiskey, who ran their stills by moonlight because the smoke would give them away by day, as Difford's Guide tells it. Yet the jar is made in Kentucky, not Georgia, by Heaven Hill, the Bardstown house that five brothers of the Shapira family and a group of local investors founded in 1935, filling its first barrel that December. On 7 November 1996 a fire took Heaven Hill's distillery and seven of its rickhouses. In 1999 the house bought the Bernheim distillery in Louisville from United Distillers and moved its distilling there, while ageing and bottling stayed near Bardstown. Through all of it Georgia Moon kept its glass mason jar and its wink of a label, less than 30 days old. In 2008 Heaven Hill added two flavoured versions at 70 proof in the same jar, and a stronger Fruit Jar at 100 proof stands beside the original in some markets. Behind a bar Georgia Moon is the lawful face of moonshine: a corn whiskey, taxed and labelled, that has spent almost no time in wood, and a plain way to show a guest what corn tastes like before the barrel.

records.story: Moonshine in the Tennessee hills was often corn whiskey made out of the taxman's sight and sold clear and young. Even after national Prohibition ended, Tennessee kept lawful distilling within narrow bounds: before 2009 it was allowed in only three counties, Moore, Coffee and Lincoln, the homes of Jack Daniel's, George Dickel and a rum distillery. In 2009 the legislature opened distilling to 41 more counties, those where liquor was already served by the drink, and Sevier County was among them. Ole Smoky opened in the mountain town of Gatlinburg in 2010, on the weekend of 4 July as one account has it. It set out to make the hills' own spirit lawfully: corn whiskey, clear and unaged, in a glass jar, from what the house calls a recipe a hundred years old, which is its own claim and not a matter of record. Flavoured jars followed the Original, and more distilleries in Tennessee followed the one in Gatlinburg. For a bartender the Original is the moonshine a guest names, and the plain proof that a lawful jar of moonshine is corn whiskey that never met a barrel.

records.story: Two brothers of the Holladay family founded a distillery at a limestone spring in Weston, Missouri, in 1856. One brother handed it to the other in 1860, and after him a son-in-law ran it until a sale in 1900 made it the Shawhan Distillery. Through Prohibition it stayed open by bottling whiskey already made, for medicinal use. After a sale in 1936 it became the Old Weston Distillery, and in 1942 the McCormick name, bought from a plant at nearby Waldron, gave the company the title McCormick Distilling. Under that name the company sent out Platte Valley, a straight corn whiskey in a ceramic jug sealed with a cork; jugs from the 1960s carry age statements older than the bottling's, so the whiskey inside has changed over the years. In 2016, for the 160th year of the site, the old distillery took back the Holladay name and turned again to making bourbon. For a bartender Platte Valley is the aged corn in the jug: the bottle that shows a guest that corn whiskey can rest in oak, look like moonshine and yet not be bourbon.

records.story: Balcones was founded in Waco in 2008, in a former welding shop of about two thousand square feet, wedged against the pylons of a bridge over Waco Creek, with low ceilings and a leaking roof. Distilling began in 2009, and Baby Blue was the whisky it began with, made from roasted blue corn: as Imbibe tells it, the corn began as Hopi blue corn grown in New Mexico, before the house turned to a blue flint corn grown in West Texas. A corn whisky aged in used oak and bottled at 92 proof, it made the name of a distillery that went on to malt, rye and smoked whiskies. In 2014 the founder left after a dispute with the company's investors, and the distillery carried on without him. Between 2015 and 2016 the company refitted the Texas Fireproof Storage building in Waco, a far larger home with larger stills, and moved its distilling there. The used oak is what keeps Baby Blue a corn whisky and not a bourbon. For a bartender it is the craft answer to Mellow Corn: corn whisky made to be sipped, with the roast of the corn in the glass.
